# US military says strike disabled ship trying to run blockade on Iran
By Agencies and ToI Staff

The United States military announced late Saturday that it disabled a St. Kitts-flagged commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman after the ship's crew "ignored repeated warnings" and attempted to violate the naval blockade against Iran multiple times. According to a U.S. Central Command statement, "A U.S. military aircraft fired precision munitions at the stern" of the vessel to disable it.

The action represents the latest military engagement in an ongoing enforcement operation. U.S. forces have maintained a blockade on Iran for months in and around the Strait of Hormuz, a critical shipping corridor for global oil commerce. The previous confirmed strike on a cargo vessel occurred nearly a month prior in the Gulf of Oman.

The disclosure comes amid a pattern where U.S. Central Command has not announced certain military strikes in the region, with officials declining to confirm reports of explosions when questioned by media outlets.

Iranian state media reported Saturday evening explosions on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz and at the port of Jask, though the cause remained unclear initially. The U.S. military did not immediately respond to Associated Press inquiries regarding these reports.

Iran's military claimed that "two tankers had hit mines in the Hormuz area and caught fire," without identifying vessel flags or destinations.

President Trump confirmed Friday that the U.S. had carried out "minor" limited strikes against Iran targeting an air defense system, though U.S. Central Command declined to comment even after the president's confirmation.

Amid ongoing military operations, mediators have presented proposals aimed at addressing differences between the United States and Iran regarding Tehran's nuclear program. According to Middle East government officials, Iran is reviewing these proposals but remains unwilling to engage in nuclear negotiations until the U.S. agrees to several core Iranian demands.

Iran's key preconditions for talks include: ending the U.S. blockade on Iranian ports, lifting sanctions, unfreezing assets, providing compensation for war damages, and ending hostilities throughout the region, including Israeli operations in Lebanon.

A proposed "bridge deal" presented by Qatari mediators would implement trust-building measures over two days, including lifting the blockade and releasing frozen Iranian funds. In exchange, Iran would allow International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors at bombed nuclear sites. On day two, Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz under a modified Iran-Oman agreement.

According to the IAEA, Iran possesses 440.9 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60 percent purity—a technical step away from weapons-grade levels of 90 percent. No civilian energy application exists for uranium at such enrichment levels.

The more than eight-month conflict began February 28 when the U.S. and Israel launched operations aimed at destabilizing Iran's regime and destroying its ballistic missile and nuclear capabilities. A June memorandum of understanding between the sides quickly unraveled after accusations of violations, leaving parties in a stalemate punctuated by intermittent military engagements.

October witnessed the highest number of attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz since March, as Iran increased economic pressure on the U.S. to compel blockade removal.
